newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan tax rise seen deterring sugar imports.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan tax rise seen deterring sugar imports.

text.p: Pakistani sugar imports are likely to plunge after the government imposed a 10 percent regulatory import duty, industry sources said on Thursday.
They said many importers would now opt to sell consignments ordered before Tuesday's surprise imposition of extra duty on sugar imports, but not yet loaded for shipment.

According to the private Pakistan Sugar Mills Association (PSMA), state and private importers imported more than 500,000 tonnes of sugar in fiscal 1996/97 (July-June), compared to only 3,500 tonnes the previous year.

"Private importers had ordered an estimated 372,000 tonnes of sugar (in 1996/97), of which 186,000 tonnes was due to arrive at the start of 1997/98," PSMA secretary general Ali Qazilbash told Reuters.
He said the 10 percent duty, on top of 24 percent of other taxes on sugar imports, would effectively deter imports as traders would lose their profit margin over domestic sugar.
"The cost of imported sugar was one rupee ($0.02) to 1.50 rupees cheaper than the sugar produced by local mills," he said.
A Karachi dealer said the 10 percent duty would add at least two rupees to the landed cost of imported sugar. "The regulatory duty has wiped out the incentive to import sugar," he said.
Qazilbash said he did not foresee any sugar shortage as an estimated 825,000 tonnes was stocked at mills as of July 1, while dealers held an estimated 400,000 tonnes.
"At an average normal consumption of 225,000 tonnes a month, sugar stocks will last at least four to four and a half months," he said. By November the new crushing season will start.

He said 1996/97 production was estimated at close to 2.4 million tonnes against annual average consumption of 2.7 million tonnes. Pakistan produced 2.47 million tonnes of sugar in 1995/96 and three million tonnes in 1994/95.
"In 1997/98 we expect a better crop and higher production of 2.85 million tonnes, so there will be no need for imports," Qazilbash said.

He said the latest reports suggested about one million hectares had been sown against 970,000 hectares in 1996/97, adding that stable market rates and a higher support price had encouraged farmers to expand the area under sugar cultivation.

In May the government increased the support price for the 1997/98 (July-June) crop to 35 rupees per 40 kg from 24 last year for Punjab and North West Frontier Province and to 36 rupees from 24.50 in Sindh and Balochistan provinces.

Sugar consumption is expected to rise to 2.85 million tonnes in 1997/98 from an estimated 2.7 million tonnes this year. This includes 1.8 million tonnes for domestic use, 900,000 tonnes for industry and 150,000 tonnes for neighbouring Afghanistan.
